newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Racing ace Lauda seeks pole position in skies.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Racing ace Lauda seeks pole position in skies.

text.p: Ask any Austrian over the age of 30 what they were doing the day formula one ace Niki Lauda crashed and they will be able to recall the incident to the last detail.

Two events on the same day in August 1976 shook Austrian national identity to the core: Lauda's Ferrari exploded in a fireball on Germany's Nuerburgring and Vienna's Reichsbruecke bridge crumbled into the Danube River.

But reigning world formula one champion Lauda lived to fight another day and despite severe facial burns and damage to his lungs he snatched two more titles before finally retiring from the sport in 1985.

The 47-year-old native Viennese has since traded in life on the circuit for the cramped offices of his own airline, Lauda Air, at Vienna airport and swapped the cockpit of his racing car for the Boeing planes he regularly pilots.
"The basic principle is the same. You have to give 100 percent to win," Lauda told Reuters in an interview.

The winner of 25 formula one grands prix, sporting his trademark red baseball cap, is a familiar sight on Vienna streets and a regular breakfast guest at the chic Imperial Hotel on the tree-lined Ringstrasse.
From an unimposing building overlooking the runway, the calm punctuated by the roar of jet engines, Lauda oversees a fleet of 19 planes carrying one million passengers a year.
Lauda Air is one of Austria's most high-profile companies and the nation's most celebrated entrepreneur has grown used to comparisons with Virgin Airlines founder Richard Branson.
Both men fought long battles to break the stranglehold of their respective national carriers.
"But Branson's dispute was with British Airways. Here the confrontation was with politicians who were not capable of liberal thinking," Lauda noted.

Jets called Freddy Mercury, Bob Marley, John Lennon, Janis Joplin and Leonard Bernstein give clues to Lauda's eclectic musical taste. They are joined on the tarmac by racing hero Ayrton Senna and screen idols Marilyn Monroe and James Dean.
Cabin crews wear jeans and baseball caps -- the antithesis of Austrian formality. A top Vienna restaurant supplies the food served on real plates. Not a plastic fork in sight.
"That's our product. With Lauda you get more for the same price," Lauda said, taking a pop at his present enemies, foreign state subsidised carriers.
The airline's beginnings in 1979 were humble -- two 44-seat Fokker aircraft offering flights from Salzburg were little more than a flea bite to then state monopoly Austrian Airlines.
"I experienced two years of hell because politically there was no room for a second airline in Austria," Lauda recalled.
Financial problems forced him back on to the race track in 1981, where he sealed his third world championship before returning to the airline with new vigour three years later.

"The experience of the first two years taught me not to accept second place to Austrian Airlines but to compete with them," Lauda said, referring to the war he waged with politicians to gain a worldwide licence for scheduled flights.
The man his racing critics once compared to a computer freely admits he is a tough task master to his 1,200 employees, working on the premise: if I can do it so can others.

And he acknowledges the past 20 years has had its dark side. Lauda has said he was close to throwing in the towel in 1991 when one of his airplanes plunged into the bamboo jungles of northern Thailand, killing all 223 on board.
He responds with irritation to questions about his company's "disappointing" performance in the first half of this year, when Lauda Air's pre-tax loss deepened some 80 percent.
"The first half is disappointing for every airline because it includes the winter months," he said curtly.

Lauda is confident his business can thrive in an increasingly competitive global market, backed by the muscle of Germany's Lufthansa which has a 39.7 percent stake. The firm is eagerly awaiting the delivery later this year of a new Boeing 777.
"That will give us more capacity. At present we can only fulfil our existing timetable," Lauda explained.
A hectic schedule has not prevented him from staying in touch with his first love, motor racing. Since 1992 he has juggled his airline business with a consultancy job at Ferrari.
He rates Michael Schuhmacher as the best of the current generation of drivers and says Damon Hill has had the good fortune to be backed by the technical excellence of the Williams team.
"When I drove there were always three or four drivers who were competitive. Now there's just one -- Michael Schuhmacher... But Hill has found the best package," he said.
While he remembers fondly distant tussles with James Hunt, Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost, Lauda does not miss the risks associated with the sport of the 1970s, however.
"In my time at least one driver had a fatal accident each year...I can list them. Nowadays cars are so well built that virtually nothing goes wrong," he said.
Lauda, now divorced with two children, is adamant that his future lies with his airline and dismisses Austrian press reports that he is pitching for the job of Ferrari sports chief.
"Ferrari is a sideline and that is what it will remain. This is where I work now," Lauda said, indicating his modest office, packed with filing cabinets.
"I have the freedom to decide what I do with my life and that means a great deal to me. As long as I enjoy what I am doing here, I will give it 100 percent."
